codex.worst_flaw: The company-wide rollout introduces the payout alongside workflow improvements without a comparison group, so it cannot tell whether the payout improves verified completion enough to justify its cost.

claude.worst_flaw: The incentive launches company-wide right after a two-week baseline, with no comparison group and no predefined success, cost or harm decision rules, so it cannot tell what the reward adds beyond paid checklist time, the app prompt and fixes to the workflow.

holistic.reason: Union-co-designed, safety-stop credit, offline fallback, sampling audits and a taper-with-friction-fixes plan are strong, but the reward is only about one hour of pay per block, which may feel small and go unnoticed, and the follow-up is thin on how habits persist beyond the pay.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch blocker: The design does not specify who must pause the incentive, what evidence triggers a pause, or when it can resume if technicians rush checks, conceal hazards, or face pressure to start unsafe work.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison group or isolation of the reward's incremental value over plain support. Barrier fixes, training and the reward all start together, so any adoption gain cannot be attributed and there is no predefined decision rule on cost or harm.

holistic.reason: Union-agreed, safety-protective design with fallbacks, appeals and no rankings is highly approvable, but a one-hour reward is modest and the plan is long and complex to communicate, and durability rests on the checklist becoming standard practice and barriers being fixed rather than on the incentive itself.

claude.worst_flaw: The rollout depends on a before/after comparison with no control or staggered group, so the bonus's added value over plain workflow support can't be separated from novelty, the paid time or the app fixes. On top of that, the fixed 90% weekly threshold creates all-or-nothing cliffs for technicians with only a few jobs a week.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot lacks a stop rule for backfilled safety checks or pressure to clear unsafe jobs, leaving a safety risk that should block launch.

holistic.reason: Union-agreed, paid-time, outcome-neutral design with strong data and failure-mode safeguards is approvable, but a $15 weekly bonus is modest and habit persistence after the bonus ends depends on keeping the workflow easy.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison condition or predefined decision rule beyond a before/after against a recalculated four-week baseline, so it cannot tell whether the reward added anything beyond the rotation and queue, and it gives no rules for leave, outages, data corrections or appeals.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the reward alongside the review rotation, shared queue, and reminders, so it cannot tell whether the reward adds value beyond those workflow changes.

holistic.reason: Team-wide reward, transparent rules, quality audits and a rotation address sceptic concerns and gaming risks well, but the half-day is a modest incentive and complex rules plus a 90% target may feel heavy, with gains likely to fade once the reward ends unless the rotation and queue stay.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward runs alongside the new review rotation and reminders without a comparison group, so the pilot cannot tell whether the reward adds value.

claude.worst_flaw: The pilot has no comparison and no isolation of the incremental value of the reward over the rotation and queue, so a before/after change cannot be credited to the incentive, and there are no replayable records, permission rules or staffed appeal path to audit the on-time scoring.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with fair measurement, anti-gaming audits, workload safeguards and a team-wide reward that suits sceptical engineers, though a single half-day payout and a pilot that ends after one decision may not sustain the habit once the incentive is gone.

claude.worst_flaw: The design checks success only against a before/after baseline. It has no comparison group or plain-support arm, so it cannot tell whether the half-day reward adds anything beyond the rotation and queue. It also lacks replayable event history, permissions and an appeal process for disputed timestamps or quality failures.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the reward, review rotation, queue, and alerts together, so its historical baseline cannot establish whether the reward adds value over the workflow changes alone.

holistic.reason: A well-specified, sceptic-friendly pilot with team-level non-cash reward, quality checks, and protected duty time is easy to approve, but it is complex enough that attention may fade and the behaviour depends on the rotation and alerts continuing after the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: Without a plain-feedback comparison, the pilot cannot determine whether the team reward improves logging beyond feedback and kiosk workflow fixes.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never tests whether the kiosk adds value over the existing observer audit: there is no comparison arm and no predefined outcome or decision threshold, and the kiosk logging may itself be low-value work that takes nurses away from care.

holistic.reason: The design is rigorous, safety-conscious and guards well against gaming, but the heavy audit-reconciliation burden and a modest one-off team reward with no live feedback give it low salience, and the behaviour is likely to fade once the incentive is retired.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch blocker: The design sets no acceptable false-match rate for the ward, category, and time matching that determines reward eligibility.

claude.worst_flaw: The pilot has no comparison against plain feedback with no reward, and it does not measure logging after the reward is retired, so it cannot show what the incentive added or whether logging lasts.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with independent audit matching, clinical safeguards and no individual pressure, but it is complex to administer, the €250 team reward is modest and likely invisible to busy nurses, and with the incentive retired after four months, kiosk logging may fade unless it proves its worth.

claude.worst_flaw: All three wards get the incentive, so there is no comparison group or plain-feedback arm; the design can only compare before and after and cannot show that the reward or kiosk added value beyond the audit and huddle support.

codex.worst_flaw: All three wards receive the reward offer, so the pilot cannot isolate its effect from kiosk rollout, practice, and feedback.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, audit-anchored team reward with sound safeguards against gaming and privacy risk, but €300 is small, the logging burden is real, and the incentive expiring after month 4 with no built-in habit support makes durable logging behaviour after the pilot uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: Without a comparison group receiving the same workflow support and private feedback, the pilot cannot tell whether the team reward improves verified coverage.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison group and no predefined decision rule, so it cannot separate the incentive's added value from plain coaching or a secular trend; a single team-wide 80% target also ignores uneven queue volume and case mix, and gives no individual next step after a missed week.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded against gaming with audits, customer guardrails and a clean ending, but a two-hour learning reward for a team-wide 80% threshold from a 12% baseline is weak and distant, so awareness and motivation are modest and the habit may fade once the incentive expires.

codex.worst_flaw: The 85% payout threshold counts legitimate exceptions in the denominator without first measuring how often an article is applicable, so agents could handle every eligible ticket correctly and still miss the target.

claude.worst_flaw: There is no comparison group or plain-support arm, so the design cannot separate the incentive's effect from the workflow changes or from case mix. It only defines pause triggers and never sets decision criteria tied to cost or sample size.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded design with a shared reward, audits, quality gates, and a retained workflow, but the incentive is only two hours of paid time, the programme is complex, and a shared team goal can weaken individual motivation and leave quiet agents free-riding.

codex.worst_flaw: The payout metric can overstate verified coverage because QA checks only a sample of exemptions and the formula leaves wrongly exempted tickets outside the denominator unless QA catches them individually.

claude.worst_flaw: The 85% target is set before any baseline under the new eligibility rules, and success is judged only against the pre-launch period, with no comparison group. That leaves no way to tell what the reward added beyond the resolution prompt, protected writing time and editors. The all-or-nothing group reward for the last two weeks also ignores leave and outages, gives no appeal path, and lets managers use private individual results for coaching without stated limits.

holistic.reason: The design is careful about quality sampling, exemptions and service guardrails, but the reward is a single team-wide hour that is small and hard to earn, the 85% target is a big jump from 12%, and the workflow and process burden are heavy, so I expect the behaviour to fade once the reward ends.
